15. What's Going on With The Impeachment

The impeachment trial, as it stands, is a little bit of a mess, with what feels like many muddled and ever-changing accusations, against a president who keeps doing new things to be accused of. Right now Nancy Pelosi orchestrated an impeachment vote in the house, but has stalled refusing to send a vote to the senate. Given all the confusion I'd like to take a step back to understand how we got here, and why it all happened the way it did.

Before anything, we need to understand that this is first and foremost a popularity contest, with a jury of the American public. There are legal rules, sure, but the people who are voting on impeachment are congressmen, and congressmen represent the desires of their constituents. You can see this in the correllation between congressmen's willingness to defend Trump and his popularity within their home state, as well as how their treatment of him changed as he rose in popularity within the republican party. In order to get him impeached, the Democrats need to convince the people that he should be removed from office.

8.1 The Russia Investiagtion

On November 8, 2016 Democrats were absolutely stunned. Despite all the polls from trustworthy sources like the New York Times*, an unthinkable candidate had won the election. There had to have been a mistake. There had to have been something deeply wrong, Democrats everywhere searched for an explanation.

Not believing that such a candidate could have won fairly, they blamed James Comey for unfairly reporting on Hillary's e-mails just days before the election. They blamed misleading polls discouraging Democrats from voting in an already "certain" election. And finally, they blamed Russia for interfering in our Democratic process, certain that for this to happen, rules must have been deeply and influentially broken.

There was a lot of evidence suggesting wrongdoing. Trump always seemed to have a soft spot when he spoke of Russia. There were the meetings in Trump tower. And Trump seemed to be doing everything in his power to kill the investigation.

The first weeks of Trump's administration were hectic to say the least. Trump picked fights with anyone and everyone. He struggled to assemble a cabinet and wound up leaving many key government positions unfilled. He seemed hell-bent on ignoring all rules and structure, as much as he possibly could. And finally, in a move that shocked many, he fired the person investigating him, FBI director James Comey.

Things moved quickly. Deputy Attorney Rod Rosenstien appointed a special counsel to replace Comey in the Russia investigation. Mueller seemed like just the man for the job, and over the coming weeks, his team gained momentum. Democrats saw not only mountains of evidence piling up, but real criminal offenses, with Mueller and his team reaching indictment after indictment. And Trump, although powerless to fire Mueller seemed to be doing everything in his power to kill the investigation.

The Democrats saw the way the investigation was going, and they saw the indictments lining up, and they made a crucial tactical error. Instead of zeroing in on the firing of Comey, the offense they knew he had committed, they threw all their efforts behind the Russia investigation, doing everything possible to stoke public excitement for a dramatic Mueller testimony.

They had a precedent from the Nixon investigation, one of the few issues on which Trump lacked positive sentiment within the Republican party, and what looked to be an undeniable act of treason. They thought the Mueller report was going to be a bombshell. That they were going to catch Trump red-handed, and that it would suddenly and dramatically sway public opinion. They were expecting something so severe that it would be impossible to claim impeachment was a purely partisan investigation. Even many Republicans were holding their words, waiting to see what the report described.

A week before the report's release, the Democrats made another tactical error. Instead of demanding Mueller first testify to the public directly, they allowed his report to pass, largely unquestioned, through Trump's justice department, and Attorney General William Barr. I don't know if they could have stopped Barr from publishing his letter, but they could have kept the tension, pushing people to wait for the bombshell that was the final report. Instead, they let the singular news story, the one they were building up for months, be not Mueller's report itself, but Barr's report on Mueller's report.

8.2 The Mueller Report

On March 24, 2019, Barr issued his letter to Congress. The verdict was "no collusion", i.e. the investigation did not establish coordination between Trump and the Russian government. Importantly, despite all the evidence in the report, Barr himself decided that Trump had not committed obstruction of justice, and attached his own findings, instead of the report's in his letter. Mueller himself described Barr's letter as a mischaracterization of his report, and in another mistake, Mueller expressed his discontent privately instead of immediately going to the public.

It was only after the full report was released, nearly a month later, that people began to realize what happened. Most neutral media organizations and fact checkers described Barr's letter to be intentionally misleading. Instead of "totally exhonerating" the president, Mueller had carefully layed out the case for obstruction of justice, and seemed only to not reach a verdict because it was not in the mandate for his report. In addition, instead of finding no evidence of direct collusion, he did suggest there was questionable behavior towards Russia.

By this point the moment had long since passed. Democrats had been hyping up a jarring news story, and what they got was a drawn out fizzle. There was a lot of dirt in the Mueller report, but Democrats didn't get the conclusive proof they claimed was lurking. They tried to pivot and push further, but having failed the first time, it looks like they were just grasping at ways to accuse the president.

If they had focused in on obstruction of justice, they would have gotten the president on an act they knew he had committed, and bad news from the Russia investigation wouldn't have broken their momentum. On the other hand, if they had spent months arguing that Trump had broken rules by firing Comey, and real evidence was found from the Russia investigation it still would have been the bombshell they needed to sway public sentiment and press further. This is again an instance where Democratic leadership was too confident and failed to plan effectively to minimize their downside.

8.3 Rebuilding a Case

In the months after the Barr's letter, the Democrats were frustrated and disorganized. They sensed Trump was doing something wrong still, and pushing the boundries, but they lacked a single rallying cry. If they had done so from the beginning, their strongest play would have been to rally around the firing of James Comey, but by now years had passed, and it would be hard to pick back up again.

Despite the lack of a central rallying cry Democratic voters were angry, and they were growing more angry with each new presidential offense. More and more moderate Democrats, long evasive, now publically voiced their support for impeachment. As primary season rolled in, all eyes turned to the candidates, who felt rising pressure from the left-most wing of the party. Unable to avoid the question in debate after debate, the candidates all lined up in support of impeachment. Only Nancy Pelosi and her closest allies held their breath.

8.4 The Ukraine Scandal

Finally, in September, news broke that President Trump asked the Ukranian government to investigate Hunter Biden the son of his chief political rival. Abuse of power to investigate a political oponent drew such a parallel to Watergate that it immediately set off alarm bells in politician's minds. Not only did they have more evidence of wrongdoing, but their anger had a central focus once again. Pelosi, sensing a shift in momentum, announced that she would begin the impeachment process. After an announcement from their extremely cautious, yet trusted leader, the rest of the Democratic party followed suit.

Why was Pelosi cautious for so long? I think it's because you only get one shot to announce articles of impeachment (or at least, if your first attempt fails, it makes your second attempt harder). I think she was saving it, waiting for a news story like this one to break, so that when something like this did come out, she could investigate it and apply pressure on it. Starting an impeachment proceding draws national news coverage, and she wanted an event that the American people would see as definitely wrong, something that was worth spending her news coverage on.

The impeachment process also makes it easier for the Democrats to carry out a formal investigation. This means that the democrats got to learn about the Ukraine scandal in more detail, and potentially uncover even more damaging information. In addition, waiting for so long gave some kind of additional credibility to the investigation. It sends the message that Pelosi feels "we don't want to do this, and we won't unless we really have to, but as it turns out we really have to."

In addition, Pelosi learned from the mistakes of the Russia investigation. Despite gaining such a powerful rallying cry, she didn't make the impeachment entirely reliant on proving coordination with Ukraine. She included an article "Obstruction of Congress", about Trump's efforts to block investigation, which relies almost entirely on publically available knowledge. As such, it can't be easily disproven, so Democrats can keep pushing in that direction no matter what other information comes out.

8.5 The Threshold of Popular Support

Despite all this, Nancy Pelosi is stuck. One of the reasons why she stalled on starting the impeachment process for so long is she knew that she wouldn't be able to carry it through to completion. At least not through the Reupblican controlled Senate, where Mitch McConnel has promised a speedy acquittal. And yet, she still wanted to start the impeachment process so that she could draw public attention and promote an investigation. So, she drafted the articles of impeachment, got them passed in the house, and then, did the only thing that she could do. She stalled. Hearing Mitch McConnel's vow, she refused to send the articles of impeachment to the senate. This means that Mitch can't kill the impeachment, and she gets to keep up the pressure until the tide turns in her favor.

What gives? Trump is an unpopular president. Just a month after he took office, over 50% of people disapproved of his presidency, according to polling tracked by 538. As of this moment, more Americans support impeaching Trump than those who are against it. Congressional votes are largely determined by the opinions of their voter-base. So why can't Pelosi get the votes she needs?

Well, impeachment is very popular among Democratic voters, but as you might have guessed, it's not very popular among Republican voters. And the thing is, it's Republican senators that need to vote for impeachment for the thing to pass. 50% of people might want Trump impeached, but that breaks down to like 80% of Democrats and only 10% of Republicans. Republican senators likely won't support impeachment unless a majority of their own party supports it. That means Trump has to be really unpopular.

Given the unwavering support of his base, it's not clear what it would take to move the needle on impeachment. Polls show an uptick in support for impeachment after news of the Ukraine scandal broke, but only a small uptick, and one that still gives impeachment less than 10% support among Republicans. If anything, the history behind the impeachment proceedings, and the haphazard way in which it all went down made it much harder to impeach Trump because it gave wiggle room for his most ferverent supporters to believe it was all just a partisan mess. I don't think it'll go anywhere in the near future, because if Pelosi is smart, she'll hold her cards and continue to prevent a Senate vote, and if Trump doesn't make any big mistakes, he likely won't lose enough popular support to be impeached.

I think going forward, the stalemate will continue. Pelosi doesn't have the votes, and shouldn't risk a clean shot at impeaching the president. Senate Republicans might try to entice her with the promise of additional testimony in the house trial, but I think Pelosi would be stupid to take it. I think Pelosi is going to wait for the next big bombshell, and then pull the trigger whenever the momentum swings.

16. Treating Cancer with Chemo (Part 3)

In this section, we now look at the specific drugs we would need to put the ideas in Part 2 into practice. We have a tremendous advantage here because we are not developing new chemicals. All of the drugs listed have already seen clinical use. What we'd like to do is, send a signal that tells all the cells in your body to start dividing, and then send a chemotherapy drug which kills any cells that are still dividing. Your body has many types of signals which tell cells when to grow and divide,

notes: platelts come from Megakaryocytes which come from hematopoietic stem cells

I found the paper that has this idea https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8839398

17. Treating Cancer with Chemo (Part 2)

In the last section we looked into what types of cancer treatments are out there, and, from a research perspective, what areas hopefully have the most low hanging fruit. Due to cancer heterogeneity, and the problem of targeting undetectable or microscopic tumors, black-box chemotherapy methods seemed like they would yield the best results. I wrote down the definition of our "black box" and narrowed in on one property, that cancer cells divide regardless of external signaling.

Many drugs already target this pathway. Certain drugs attack cells which divide more rapidly, intentionally causing damage to cells during the process of cell division. In theory this will cause cancer cells to die because they will be more likely to die than the normal cells.

The problem is, this also kills healthy cells. Some cells, such as bone marrow cells, divide rapidly and, some cancers don't even grow that quickly. Some cancers grow at a normal rate for cells, they just don't stop growing when they're supposed to. The problem is that what you want to measure is not the cancer's rate of growth, but it's responsiveness to external signals within the body.

So how can we target this? How do we identify cells which don't respond to signals?

Well, instead of targeting cancer cells, we can send signals to identify healthy cells. We know that the healthy cells will respond to the signals and the cancer cells won't. By targeting everything else, we can measure when something doesn't respond to the signals that it's supposed to, and then go after it. Instead of attacking cells that divide quickly, we can tell all of the cells to stop dividing, and then kill all the cells that still divide. The cancer cells won't listen, but the normal cells will, so they won't get the damage that usually comes with intensive chemotherapy.

What's completely wild about this to me is that people are doing this already, but not on the cells that actually matter. We treat hair loss. We can help people not lose all their hair who are going through chemo by having them apply ice packs to the top of their head while they're receiving treatment. This works by slowing the division of the cells around your hair follicles, so they won't actually get killed and fall out while you're getting treatment.

In the same way that we treat hair loss, we can tell the cells in your bone marrow to stop dividing as quickly while the chemo is active and thus drastically reduce the side effects. Furthermore, we'd be able to use drugs that weren't previously available because even though they killed the cancer they were otherwise too toxic to the human body. Even better, we already have the tools to do this. We already have drugs which slow the growth of bone marrow cells. We just have to apply them in the right way.

18. Treating Cancer with Chemo (Part 1)

Cancer treatment is something I've thought about a lot recently, and the more I've studied it, the more I've seen that it's an interesting and complex problem. At it's core a cancer is a group of cells whose genetic code has mutated such that they divide uncontrollably, in a way that cannot be properly regulated by the body. Cancer cells, in contrast to benign tumors, also have the ability to sustain their growth, and to invade other parts of the body. If the cancer cells grow too much, they can "crowd out" other bodily functions, by having large tumors that press against vital organs, or "replace" other healthy cells.

The challenge with treatment is that cancer cells, unlike bacteria or viruses, look remarkably like healthy human cells. It's difficult to kill the cancer cells without accidentally killing the normal cells. As a result, the main treatment options for cancer are:

  • Surgery: Cancers typically grow as a cluster of cells in the same physical location, called a tumor. One way to treat this is to just cut out the tumor. This is good because it can quickly and fully remove the entire tumor, but bad because it might not be in a place you can safely reach with a knife, and bad because it doesn't catch it if the cancer spread without your knowledge.
  • Radiation: Radiation zaps the cancer with high intensity beams of light. Think a really powerful microwave pointed directly at your tumor. This is good because it kills cells in places that aren't easy to reach with a knife, and can cover a wider area than would be safe to cut out, but bad because it might not kill everything in its beam and again, it won't catch the cancer if it spreads.
  • Chemotherapy: This is a broad term that refers to using chemicals to kill, or otherwise harm the cancer cells. Since this refers to many different types of chemicals, which act in many different types of ways, it's hard to give a one-size-fits all explanation. One type of chemical which is fairly common essentially tries to kill cells which are dividing very quickly or haphazardly, hoping to target the cancer cells unctonrollable growth. Chemotherapy is great because unlike radiation or surgery, it can attack cancer cells anywhere in the body, meaning that if the tumor had spread to a small undetectable cluster of cells, chemotherapy would still fight it. The downside of chemotherapy is it's not always very good at determining which cells are cancer cells. This means it can kill healthy cells all over your body, most notably in the bone marrow, which tends to replenish quickly.

There are a few other types of treatments, such as immunotherapy, which I'll skip for now as largely niche (but growing) fields.

I'd like to focus here on chemotherapy because, while currently surgery and radiation are often necessary, because they are unable to attack small groups of cells, I don't believe that in the future, anything more than incremental progress will be made. Whatever the solution is will likely have to be some sort of medicine because we can't physically target something we don't have the ability to detect.

Medicines that treat cancer (even including immunotherapy) are hard to make because it's hard for anything to classify whether or not a cell is cancerous. So, in order to treat cancer, we need to solve the classification problem, build a model to predict whether or not a cell is cancerous, and then encode it on a macroscopic scale. The more accurate our model, the more likely that the drug will kill the cancer without being otherwise fatal to the human body.

We can approach this classification as a "black box", i.e. the cell is a generic thing with certain properties which we can't see into. Or, we can think of it as an open box, i.e. the mutated DNA of a cancer cell causes these specific chemical reactions which, eventually cause the cell to divide uncontrollably. With open box models, we have a tremendous amount more information that we can use to classify the cell as dangerous, and it seems like this would be intrinsically easier, but this information comes at a cost. Cancer is a name for a disease that can occur in many different ways and for many different reasons, often exhibiting significant heterogeneity within a single tumor. If we treat one specific pathway of chemical reactions, we'll only solve the problem for those specific cells, and we'll miss out on all the different types of cancer that are possible.

I'd like to think about this problem as a black box problem because in addition to the curse of heterogeneity, it's also just better suited to my background. Treating the cell as an open box generally means lab work with equipment I don't have access to, and at best a 5-10 year trial period before a new chemical gets into production. It's my hypothesis that there are enough building blocks that are already well studied, that if we put them together in just the right way, we'll get a better result.

So let's take a look at the black box. I took a look at the definition of a cancer cell. It boils down to roughly:

  1. The cells grow and divide regardless of what body signals them to do
  2. They don't die when they're supposed to
  3. They can invade other parts of the body
  4. They get the rest of the body to support their growth (encourage blood vessel construction)

I'd say 2 is almost impossible to go after as a black box, since you can't ask a cell whether it will die without killing it. 3 seems similarly difficult because at best it can only attack spread, and not the original tumor, and because it's hard to ask a cell where it originally came from. 4 seems promising, but again has the problem that it likely won't cure tumors of smaller than a certain size. So, all things considered, I'd like to take a closer look at 1, that cancer cells grow and divide regardless of the body's signals.

19. The Importance of Doing Nothing

This morning I woke up, a little on the later side, and didn't have anything important to do. I didn't have work, and I didn't have chores, just had to eat breakfast, and be out the door by noon. I had 2 and a half hours, so it should have been easy.

With so much time, and nothing, really, to do, I started browsing the front page of reddit. I thought maybe the act of reading, or looking at something would wake me up a little. 30 minutes passed. This was no big deal, as I had all morning, really, but I felt like I wasn't quite done yet, so I kept going.

By 1130, I was still searching for something initeresting, and I still hadn't found what I was looking for. I knew I was wasting time, and I knew that I wasn't going to feel fully satisfied at the end of it, but it always felt like the next two or three minutes would make me feel a little bit better, and that little time wouldn't be a deal breaker. By the end of it, I would click on a YouTube video and only watch the last thirty seconds of it, because in truth I didn't really want to watch the video, but I wanted to feel like I was going to find something new and entertaining. I didn't really feel like I was thinking at all, or even that I was enjoying what I was doing, but I wanted to see something. You can probably guess that I rushed the quickest breakfast (read: two bananas), and was out the door 20 minutes late.

Whenever I mess something up, I ask myself how I could of done better. In this case it seems pretty obvious. I could have just not wasted 3 hours scrolling around on the internet. I could have looked at Reddit for only an hour and a half, made myself a delicious breakfast, and still left on time.

But in practice, it's not that simple. That's because what you do with your time affects your ability to think and make decisions. If, after 90 minutes, I took a break to really sit, and think clearly about what I wanted to be doing, I would have realized I still wanted to breakfast, and that I wanted to be on time. But because I was watching videos, and because I was constantly blasting my mind with different signals, I never had a moment to really process what was going on.

Not only that, I noticed even after I left my apartment, after I had already stopped looking at a screen, I was still left with that same mentality. While I was walking to the train, I still felt this impulse to play chess or read the news. I wasn't thinking about the rest of the day, or about things I wanted to learn, or things I really cared about. For most of the afternoon, my head was still overloaded, and when I went to think, what came out were random memes and stories. I had given myself so much new information to process, that even after I was done looking at it, it still crowded out my other thoughts. It's not just about the moment, wasting your time does damage, and it's important to recognize what damage it's doing.

Maybe the videos made me feel happy for a half hour or so. Maybe I even learned a tiny bit, about news, or life advice, or something that might make good conversation. But I think I would have been better off if I had done, really, absolutely nothing. I would have been better off if I just sat down in a chair, and just waited. When I do nothing, it gives me the mental space to process longer-term thoughts, to prepare for my day, and to figure out what I really, genuinely want to be doing.

20. Why I Support Citizens United

Most people I know really don't like Citizens United. For those who aren't familiar, Citizens United was a supreme court decision that essentially let corporations and wealthy individuals funnel unlimited amounts of money into American politics. Not only that, it let people donate to certain types of political causes with little to no transparency or oversight. The people I know who don't like it view it as letting big money buy elections and spread corruption in American politics.

We have anti-bribery laws (which the courts have upheld). We have campaign finance laws (which the courts have upheld). So, what makes the Citizens United ruling different?

The Citizens United ruling applies only to campaign advertisements (not general campaign contributions), and only to money that is spent "independently", i.e. without talking directly to the candidate or political party. This means that if I'm Exxon Mobile, I still can't write Mitch McConnell a check for 10 million dollars. I also can't work with Mitch McConnel to film a TV ad for his upcoming election. But if I decide that I really like Mitch McConnel, and I don't talk to anybody, and I just pay for an ad telling everyone how great he is, then nobody can stop me.

As experience has shown, advertising can make a huge difference in the outcome of an election. If someone is allowed to spend an infinite amount of money on advertising, they, as an individual can have a massive influence on the outcome of an election. We have anti-bribery laws, but if someone can use money to ensure candidates with certain political views are elected, aren't the effects the same?

I like to think of this by considering the role of a news organization. We need some news organizations discussing American politics in order to keep voters informed, so that they can better understand the issues and decide who to vote for. Along these lines, it's even important to have news organizations that debate different topics, and to have editorials which discuss their own opinions because it's important for people to understand the reasoning behind the legislation, and get a sense of why or why not something is a good idea. Especially for traditional media outlets like newspapers and television, It's nearly impossible to publish editorials or simply report the news without incurring some sort of bias.

If you wanted to start a new cable news channel, you'd have to pay for a studio, for cable companies to distribute your broadcast, and to advertise your broadcast to others. Your news broadcast might be extremely biased, because, as we've already discussed, it's impossible to regulate bias in news organizations. You might not want a long-form news broadcast, so instead of paying for an entire television channel for an entire day, you might want to only purchase a slot that's the length of your show, or the message you want to publish. Separately, you might also want to be able to advertise your show (as news organizations are able to advertise), and in doing so accurately describe what's in it.

So, the question is, where do you draw the line? What's the difference between paying to broadcast an editorial piece and donating directly to a political campaign? Well, I think making sure that the broadcast isn't part of (organized by) the political campaign itself is a pretty fair place to draw the line.

21. Camera Settings

When I got my first DSLR, I opened up the settings menu, and found it loaded with options: active-d lighting, vignette control, auto-bracketing, ambient lighting, and much more. It took a while to sift through all the options, but after assigning some reasonable defaults (use full resolution, turn on vibration reduction when available, etc.), I found that despite all of the options, there were really only four dials that effected the raw image. The rest were either only in post-processing, or just different ways of twisting those original four dials.

Despite all the complexity, the only four dials you have on your camera are:

  1. Exposure

    Your camera has a sensor in it. When you take a picture, the camera opens up and lets light into the sensor. The longer the camera opens up, the more time light has to hit the sensor, and the brighter the overall image.

    This comes from a time before people had digital cameras. When people used film, each wave of light would cause a chemical reaction on the film, so letting in waves of light for a longer period of time would cause more chemical reactions, and all of the individual waves of light would "add together" to form the overall image. That's why if you move a camera around while the film is exposed, the image comes out blurry.

  2. Focus Distance

    In front of the sensor, your camera has a lens. The job of the lens is to take in all of the light from the outside world, and bend it, so that the light is pointed at the sensor. Typically the outside world is larger than the size of the sensor, so the lens bends the light toward the center, with the light kind of following the shape of a cone. If the lens bends the light correctly, the square of the outside world that you want to capture will hit the image like a bunch of parallel beams of light, and you'll project a much bigger image onto a much smaller sensor. However, if the cone of light is too short, or too long, instead of hitting the image like parallel lines, the beams of light will get criss-crossed. Instead of one exact point on the outside world corresponding to one exact spot on the sensor, it might miss, and send some of the light kind of nearby, causing the image to be blurry. The correct focal distance is different for objects at different distances from the camera, so if you make nearby objects in focus, you make faraway objects out of focus.

    Long story short, if a part of an image is not in focus, it looks blurry. You get to choose a distance away from the camera such that objects at that distance are in focus. The further away an object is from the focus you chose, the more blurry it looks in the photo.

  3. Aperture

    Typically, there's a physical shutter that opens up when you take a picture to let light onto the film or sensor. Aperature refers to how big of an opening there is when the shutter is open. If there's a really big hole, it lets in a lot of light, but if there's really small hole, it only lets in a little bit of light. Also, if there's a small hole, the cone of light (from the focus section) is skinnier, so the beams don't get criss-crossed as much. This means that objects that aren't at the focus distance don't wind up being as blurry, because there's less interference. If there's a big hole, the cone is wider, so only objects at a specific distance are in focus, and everything else comes out blurry. This can be useful in taking portraits when you want to emphasize an in-focus person against an out-of-focus background.

  4. ISO

    How sensitive your camera sensors are to light. High ISO means your camera registers a lot of input from a small amount of light. Most cameras are only able to get accurate readings up to a certain level of sensitivity, so bumping your ISO too high can result in noisy/grainy images.

So why do cameras have so many other options? Well, taking photos in the real world it isn't always easy to quickly and accurately adjust these four dials to set up for the shot you want. Want to get that monkey in focus? The one that's swinging across the jungle? Good luck twisting your focus knob and trying to keep up with it. You'll probably want your camera's autofocus tracking. Want to take many photos in a row, with different levels of exposure? There's a setting for that. It's not enough to just have access to those dials, you also want convenience tools that let you quickly choose how and when to take a photo.

In addition, even though it doesn't effect the raw image, many cameras have built-in post-processing to adjust for things like ambient lighting. While for more serious shots, you'll probably edit the raw files in a program on your computer like photoshop or lightroom, it is convenient, visually to get quick feedback on what the image might look like, and for those of us that are lazy out there, can be a quick way to produce reasonable quality images.

The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. This fresh start allows us to take everything we’ve learned from Thunderbird Desktop and Android to ensure a fast, reliable, and modern experience on your iPhone right from the start.

Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified. 

Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future.

Below we’ve captured some of our work in progress. Nothing is final, but we wanted to share what we are cooking up so far. If you have feedback, keep reading on. At the bottom of the post we have  a link to a user research study where we want to hear from you and what you want to see from Thunderbird for iOS.

Hassle-free setup

We know people are really busy, often doing more than one thing at a time. We’re making login fast, secure, and fully automatic, so whether you’re signing in with a single click or setting up multiple accounts, you can get to your inbox quickly. 

Solid reliable connections

An email app is only as good as its connection. Behind the scenes, we’re building a background sync that maintains a steady connection with your provider that keeps your inbox up to date while respecting your battery life.

Core daily tools

Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way.

Designed for growth

Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. This means power users will be able to test out new experimental features early, and external contributors can easily help us extend what the app can do.

When can you try it?

Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months.

Building with our community, not just for people, is core to what we are trying to do. To help us decide what to build next after our first release, we’d love your input. If you had to pick the top three things that matter most to your daily email routine, what would they be?

➡️ Survey link
Update: the survey has now closed. Thanks to all that responded!

A note to the community 

Lastly, we know how long many of you have been asking for and waiting for Thunderbird on iOS. Whether you’ve dropped a comment on our forums, tagged us on social media, or simply kept an eye on our progress, thank you for your patience!

Bringing Thunderbird to iPhone and iPad isn’t just about building an app; it’s about doing it right so it serves you reliably for years to come. Today, we want to pop open the hood, share where we are, and work with everyone to design the best possible experience.

PRESS RELEASE October 13, 2026

Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI

A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K, delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience.1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free.2
The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes.3
The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13.
“The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.”

An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence

Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.”

AuthorsJianhua Li, Yun Xing, Girisha De Silva, Ryan Flint, Kai Yuan, Sean Suchter

The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.

item.title: An hour of audio transcribed in about 13s on MacBook Air (319 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://eg2.haku.sh/, See on Hacker News

Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air, entirely on device.

Download for Mac (free) v1.6 · macOS 14+ · Apple Silicon
models download on first launch (715 MB)

Can an embedding model transcribe speech?

EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.

So we tried reading words straight out of that space.

How it works

  1. EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is.
  2. A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space.
  3. The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript.
  4. A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals.

Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months.

In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said.

In its bankruptcy filing, Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property.

Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas. Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters.

Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024.

Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

item.title: Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM (108 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.heise.de/en/news/Crypto-thieves-sell-hardware-wallets-with-secret-eSIM-11485188.html, See on Hacker News

  1. Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM
    • LTE modem calls home
    • Secret change of ownership at dealer
    • Series production

“The Ledger Nano X is the most secure way to manage your cryptocurrency,” advertises the French company Ledger, its hardware wallet for cryptocurrencies. Nevertheless, users have lost around 100 million US dollars in cryptocurrencies. This is because unknown individuals have succeeded in intercepting and manipulating the offline wallets while on the go.

Each Ledger Nano X has a Secure Element chip that controls a tiny touchscreen. Ledger praises this as particularly secure. Unfortunately, this only applies if attackers cannot read the screen. This is exactly what the perpetrators are doing. They insert additional hardware into apparently genuine Ledger Nano X and then sell them to unsuspecting crypto speculators.

If buyers use such a modified hardware wallet and create a seed phrase with it, the attackers automatically read along. They haven’t touched the Secure Element chip at all; it remains secure. Instead, they have installed an additional chip that intercepts the transmission from the Secure Element to the built-in screen and recognizes the displayed letters of the seed phrase – embedded Tempest. This is indicated by an analysis by Tibane Labs.

LTE modem calls home

Recognizing the characters alone doesn’t help the perpetrators yet, because the wallets fundamentally work offline. So the perpetrators have also installed an LTE modem, a tiny eSIM module, and a small antenna, all powered by the accumulator already built into the hardware wallet. Thus, the seed phrase is transmitted via mobile phone to the perpetrators, who thus gain control over the cryptocurrency assets secured by the seed phrase.

Ledger has admitted to one customer that they suffered financial loss and that their hardware wallet was manipulated. However, the company has not yet confirmed the exact circumstances and the full extent of the damage. Blockchain observers state that they have identified over 300 affected wallets so far, which have been collectively depleted of approximately 93 million US dollars. The stolen cryptocurrency units are subsequently exchanged and, at least in part, laundered through crypto mixers.

Secret change of ownership at dealer

Suspicion is directed at Cryptobilis, a wallet dealer operating primarily in Southeast Asia from Malaysia. Anyone who has purchased from Cryptobilis in the last three months should not use these wallets and should quickly move any existing holdings to another wallet, Ledger advises. It prohibits Cryptobilis from making further sales for now. All Ledger dealers are prohibited from offering any returns to other customers.

Unfortunately, not every affected buyer knows that they bought from Cryptobilis. Tibane Labs reports a manipulated Ledger device that was purchased via Amazon Japan from a Chinese seller but was mailed in Malaysia.

In the crypto scene, it is said that Cryptobilis recently received new owners without this being announced. The previous owners reportedly state they have nothing more to do with their old company. According to unverified screenshots, the wallet dealer has belonged to a Chinese man named JiaMing since August. Depending on the pronunciation, this is a common name in China or means “wrong name”.

Series production

The recently discovered manipulated Ledger devices are at least the third generation. In May, embedded specialist Joe Grand presented at the Hardware.io conference, apparently Ledger Nano[ ]X still manipulated by hand. To make space in the small USB stick, the perpetrators replaced the accumulator with a much smaller one and created conspicuous wiring – conspicuous, of course, only if you take the USB stick apart, which users don’t usually do.

Tibane Labs now describes wallets of two further advanced manipulation generations. One was already more professionally designed but still replaced the battery. In the third known generation, added parts are precisely cut in professional series production, and the original battery is untouched.

The perpetrators have found another, less conspicuous way: Ledger protects the built-in screen from below with foam. The attackers scratch this away and thus create space for their additional hardware. Anyone who opens the casing will see nothing other than unmanipulated Ledger Nano X, except for a small antenna wire.

item.title: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey (295 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.thehistoryblog.com/archives/77107, See on Hacker News

Archaeologists have uncovered a royal archive of cuneiform tablets in the ancient Hittite city of Samuha, modern-day Sivas, central Turkey. This year’s excavation unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments which record an epidemic of fever, military logistics, religious practices and events of royal daily life 3,400 years ago. Last year’s excavation uncovered 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments, so this season’s discoveries more than triple the number of texts. It is now the largest, most comprehensive archive of Hittite-language documents found in the 21st century.

The records date to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, and are written in Hittite and Hurrian. One text tells of a fever epidemic that struck the infant daughter of the king. She was still a nursing baby when she became ill. She never recovered from the fever and her health declined precipitously until she passed away. The cuneiform tablet records the funerary ritual that followed.

The health of the princes and princesses, not just babies but even up to adulthood, was an important focus of the records. The children of high-ranking imperial officials were given the same attention. Because illness was considered an expression of divine will, religious leaders performed many rituals to keep an eye on the physical health of the children of kings and government officials.

Another notable document is a letter from Hittite generals in western Anatolia appealing to the king for reinforcements in men, horses and chariots to fend off enemy forces. The generals’ warnings are dire. They plead that without an infusion of strength, the army would be destroyed by the enemy. They have the temerity to disclaim all responsibility for any upcoming failures if the reinforcements don’t come.

It’s a rare glimpse into the realities of military logistics with armies long distances from the king and court. The text also confirms that the king was at Samuha when the letter arrived, underscoring the city’s political importance. It was a royal stronghold for King Tudhaliya during times of military and political upheaval. His successor Suppiluliuma I used it as a launching pad for military campaigns that consolidated and expanded the territory of the Hittite Empire.

Samuha was also a major center of religious administration. Its patron deity was the goddess Sauska, goddess of love and war who was the Hurrian version of Ishtar and the most important goddess in the Hurrian pantheon. The association with the goddess was central to the city’s identity and was reflected in its religious ceremonies.

One tablet records the journeys of bird diviners who left Samuha and traveled through different regions. Their routes, the cities where they stayed and the birds they observed were recorded in a format resembling a diary. The documents also provide previously unknown information about how bird omens were observed, evaluated and interpreted by the Hittites.

The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture.

item.title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF (103 pts)

The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.

In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.

Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”

An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.

It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.

The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.

“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.

Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.

The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.

Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.

The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.

Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.

The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.

In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.

In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.

It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.

It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.

In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.

He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.

“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

item.title: A look at OpenAI’s math that’s claimed computes faster Fourier transforms (231 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.argmin.net/p/faster-fourier-transforms, See on Hacker News

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product.1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:

For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n2 arithmetic operations.

The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965.2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log2(n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log2(n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log2(n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time. All constants are equivalent.

Big-O notation is useful for shortcuts in algorithmic accounting, but it also allows for remarkable logical laziness. If we want a practically faster FFT, we want an algorithm that requires fewer than 50n operations for reasonably sized n. But O(n) does not mean 50 n. It could mean 1080 n. This would be considered a “linear time” algorithm. An algorithm that requires n + 1080 is also considered a linear time algorithm in the big-O regime. An algorithm that only has linear-time guarantees when n is greater than 1080 is also considered linear time. 1080 is approximately equal to the number of atoms in the known universe. That is why Richard Lipton and Ken Regan call algorithms with unfathomably large hidden constants galactic algorithms.

The OpenAI FFT algorithm is definitely galactic. The estimated values for C were 10100 when N=1012. So even when n=10100, the venerable Cooley-Tukey-Gauss FFT would be 1099 times faster.

So why is this new FFT result interesting? Well, note that in big-O notation, it is technically asymptotically faster than the Cooley-Tukey algorithm because

I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need

whatever the hell that number means.

Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.

“The model uses exact complex arithmetic.” That means it assumes you can store and multiply complex numbers at arbitrary precision. Indeed, the algorithm requires you to multiply complex numbers whose magnitudes grow superpolynomially with n. If you stored these numbers as bits, the memory requirement would effectively be exponential in the input length. It assumes you can multiply such arbitrarily large complex numbers together in a single operation. We do not have computers that can do this. So even if this theorem in main.pdf is “true” (no one knows, and I don’t care), it’s not actually solving the problem we set out to solve when looking for a faster FFT.

For people familiar with theoretical analyses of the FFT, that you need an absurd model of computation to break the FFT speed limit isn’t surprising. In 1973, Jacques Morgenstern proved that you couldn’t get a Fourier transform faster than ½ n log n if you required that complex coefficients used in the computation had bounded magnitude. That should have been the end of the story! But it wasn’t. People said Morgenstern’s restricted coefficient model was too restrictive. Forty years later, Nir Ailon showed that you couldn’t compute an FFT faster than n log n without severe numerical instabilities. This was also too restrictive for some people, I guess.

This new OpenAI result is thus less a mathematical breakthrough and more an oddity of computer scientists being bad at formalizing their design specifications. The “theoretical” definition of a computer is very far removed from the computers we actually build. The “faster” Fourier transform is merely an example where theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle. The solution is like what happens when you set computational bot streams at impossible problems and find them engaging in illegal hacking.

Many of the other “big” results in this OpenAI slopository could be critiqued in the same way. For example, one of those results was a galactic algorithm to multiply two matrices in O(n^2.25) operations. The construction used in the paper does not let you even estimate the constant that hides inside big O.3 It may as well be infinite, computable only with the divine music of the spheres.

Still, if written substantially better, these papers would have made it into the most prestigious publication venues for the theory of computer science (i.e., refereed conference proceedings from STOC or FOCS).4 The matrix multiplication paper would have likely won awards. But neither of these has anything to do with computers!

This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”

AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.

Abstract:Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. Older versions, checksums and other formats are on the releases page. Install details, upgrading from earlier builds and building from source are in Getting started.

Documentation: the SolidCraft book (user guide, developer guide and command reference; sources in docs/book).

Status: early but usable for simple parts. 75 of 76 public reference parts match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box (docs/oracle.md); the other is a tracked bug. These checks do not establish complete geometric or workflow equivalence. The commands SolidCraft has are listed by area in docs/features.md; status and plans are in ROADMAP.md. Open work and known bugs are in GitHub issues, and help is welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Built with SolidCraft

SELENE, a scientific rover built entirely through SolidCraft's MCP server by @0xlillith: 3,323 editable timeline steps that rebuild with no errors, replayed here at 2× speed. Full video · download the editable model.

What works

  • Sketches on origin planes, offset planes or planar faces: lines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons, slots, ellipses, fit/control splines, conics and text; construction geometry, projection, trimming, fillets and chamfers, including corners at the origin. New face attachments retain supported construction identities and chosen occurrences; missing sources expose an explicit plane repair workflow. See face attachments. Explicitly closed fit splines and closed associative offsets use periodic C2 interpolation. Supported convex line-and-arc offsets retain their identity when an inset consumes corner arcs, and linked extrusions follow the current boundary. Breaking the association freezes the boundary and keeps existing extrusions usable. Curve drawing and picking adapt together to zoom and display scale, including small circles at Fit and sketches in placed components.
  • Constraints and dimensions solved by our own solver. Points the constraints fix relative to known geometry are placed exactly by construction (loci intersections and rigid-cluster decomposition, after Owen 1991 and Fudos–Hoffmann 1997); Levenberg–Marquardt solves the rest, and the rank of its Jacobian gives the remaining degrees of freedom. Constraints: coincident, point on curve, horizontal/vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, curvature (G2), equal, concentric, collinear, midpoint, symmetry, fix; linear, aligned, horizontal, vertical, point-to-line, radius, diameter, angle, arc sweep, arc length and slot length dimensions driven by parameters. Over-constraining edits are rejected; fully constrained geometry turns black. Dragging solves the sketch every frame and rebuilds the model once, when the drag ends. Select a line or its two endpoints, type its dimension and press Enter to commit one undo step; with Sketch Dimension it's D, click, type, Enter. Fit keeps sketch geometry clear of the palette and navigation controls.
  • Profiles found automatically, including regions split by lines and holes inside outlines. Newly captured complete adaptive boundaries retain their outer and hole source identities when spline span counts change. Partial or ambiguous boundaries do not qualify.
  • Features on a parametric timeline: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet/chamfer, shell, draft, holes, threads, patterns, mirror, split, combine, move and construction geometry. The timeline rebuilds incrementally; features can be edited, suppressed, renamed, reordered and deleted. Supported geometry and current limitations are described in ROADMAP.md. New revolves preserve symmetric and two-sided angular placement across reversed axes; older designs retain their saved convention when reopened or edited.
  • Parameters and configurations with unit-aware expressions (2 * width + 5 mm, angle / 2), ordered rules, feature suppression and per-row body materials/appearances.
  • Assemblies with nested components and occurrences, joints, motion studies, contact sets, interference and material-aware mass properties. Recorded body transfers preserve modelling history and world placement; 3D sketch wires retain their coordinate frames through edits.
  • Sheet metal with flanges, hems, fold/unfold/refold, material cutouts, flat patterns, retained shallow prismatic pockets, exact line/arc/circle DXF outlines and bend tables; plastic enclosure features and rules. Pocket depth and side survive unfold/refold and appear separately from through-hole outlines in the flat preview and DXF.
  • Files: design containers (.solidcraft) with lossless binary mesh payloads; plain JSON remains supported for opening, Save As and export. Desktop Open can show a saved provisional picture from warm geometry caches while rebuilding before editing; caches never replace the parametric design. Export to STEP (AP242 with body names, colours and components as assemblies; revolved faces as native planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori), IGES 5.3 (manifold solid B-reps with names and colours), 3MF, STL (binary/ASCII) and OBJ; 3MF, STL and OBJ import as mesh bodies (they render, measure, move and export; solid features need B-rep bodies). Convert Mesh reconstructs supported closed constant-section parts as parametric solids with planar and circular cylindrical faces; STEP import (AP203/AP214/AP242 solids, assemblies, units, names, colours) and IGES import (manifold solid B-reps, or trimmed and bounded surfaces sewn into solids) as a base feature that later features build on — open a .step/.stp/.igs/.iges file, insert one into a design, or drop it on the window (docs/step-import.md).
  • Desktop app (egui + wgpu): toolbar with workspace tabs, browser, timeline, 3D viewport with axis view and navigation bar, sketch tools, feature dialogs, command palette, and a JSON-lines control channel so agents and tests can drive it. Feature errors and Help can open an editable Create Issue draft with relevant context and an optional reviewed screenshot; opening GitHub does not submit the report.
  • Headless CLI solidcraft-cli: run command scripts, measure (volume, area, centre of mass, face/edge/vertex counts), export, render PNG snapshots and replay reference recipes.
  • MCP server solidcraft-cli mcp: AI agents model, measure and look at parts headless or in the running app (see below).

Build and run

cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample          # desktop app with a sample part
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands      # the command registry
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --out bracket.step
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- snapshot examples/bracket.json --out bracket.png
cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- part.step          # open a STEP file as a new design
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- eval part.step # measure an imported STEP file
cargo xtask ci                                          # fmt, clippy, tests, assets, layers, wasm

Windows builds: cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p solidcraft.

On Windows and Linux, SolidCraft detects a connected 3Dconnexion SpaceNavigator or SpaceMouse through its multi-axis HID interface. Move the cap to pan and zoom, and tilt or twist it to rotate the 3D view. While editing a sketch, the cap pans and zooms without changing the sketch view. The Navigation page in Preferences has an on/off switch and a speed control for the 3D mouse.

On Linux SolidCraft reads /dev/hidrawN directly, so the logged-in user needs access to the device. A udev rule that adds the uaccess tag does that, for example /etc/udev/rules.d/70-3d-mouse.rules for devices with 3Dconnexion's vendor id:

SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", ATTRS{idVendor}=="256f", TAG+="uaccess"

Older SpaceNavigators use Logitech's vendor id 046d; add a rule with their product id (see lsusb) instead of matching every Logitech device. Reload with sudo udevadm control --reload && sudo udevadm trigger, then replug the device. The Flatpak sandbox does not expose hidraw devices, so the 3D mouse only works with native builds there for now. Devices that send all six axes in HID report 1 (some homemade ones do) are recognised from their report descriptor, so they work as well.

In the browser: cd apps/solidcraft-web && trunk build --release --public-url ./ (WebGPU, or WebGL2 with ?webgl; ?sample opens the sample part).

Scripts

A script is a JSON list of commands, the same ones the UI runs:

{"commands": [
  {"command": "sketch.create", "params": {"plane": "XY"}},
  {"command": "sketch.rectangle.two_point", "params": {"p0": [0, 0], "p1": [40, 30]}},
  {"command": "solid.extrude", "params": {"distance": 20}},
  {"command": "solid.fillet", "params": {"edges": [[0, 0, 10]], "radius": 3}}
]}

AI agents (MCP)

solidcraft-cli mcp is a Model Context Protocol server on stdio. Headless it runs its own design session; with --connect 127.0.0.1:PORT it drives the app started with solidcraft --control PORT, so you can watch the agent model. Tools: list_commands, execute, batch, inspect_design, measure, body_topology, set_parameter, screenshot (returns the image), export, undo, redo, new_design, open, save. Claude Code: claude mcp add solidcraft -- solidcraft-cli mcp. Details, client configuration and an example session: docs/mcp.md.

Architecture

Layer Crates Role
L0 geom vectors, planes, profiles, meshes and their measures
L1 sketch, kernel, render constraint solver and profiles; the B-rep kernel boundary (truck); view math and CPU rasterizer
L2 doc parameters, expressions, the feature timeline and its incremental evaluation
L3 io design files, STL/OBJ/STEP/3MF export, STEP and 3MF/STL import features
L4 engine the session and the command registry (everything is a command)
L5 ui-egui, mcp the swappable desktop front end; the MCP server (headless or bridged to the app)
apps solidcraft, solidcraft-cli desktop app, headless CLI

Contributing

Coming from Autodesk Fusion? SolidCraft uses familiar parametric CAD workflows: constrained sketches, solid features, an editable timeline, parameters and assemblies. See the roadmap for supported operations and current limitations.

See CONTRIBUTING.md: how to build and test, the code map, the clean-room and licence rules, and where help is wanted most.

Licence

MIT OR Apache-2.0, at your option. Developed under the clean-room contribution rules; third-party code and assets retain their documented licences and attribution.

SolidCraft is independent. Behaviour is designed from public documentation, general CAD conventions and user feedback. Reference tests use analytic values and open-source tools. SolidCraft is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by Autodesk. Autodesk and Fusion are trademarks of Autodesk, Inc.
